claim: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), is a leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide, causing approximately 10 million new cases of active TB disease and 1.5 million deaths per year.
source: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), is a leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide, causing approximately 10 million new cases of active TB disease and 1.5 million deaths per year (World Health Organization 2022, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to World Health Organization reports from 2021 and 2022.

claim: BCG protects children against disseminated Mtb infection.
source: Currently, the only clinically licensed vaccine to prevent TB is Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG), which protects children against disseminated Mtb infection (Roy et al., 2014), but provides limited and highly variable protection against pulmonary TB in adults (Fine, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roy et al., 2014.

claim: BCG provides limited and highly variable protection against pulmonary TB in adults.
source: Currently, the only clinically licensed vaccine to prevent TB is Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG), which protects children against disseminated Mtb infection (Roy et al., 2014), but provides limited and highly variable protection against pulmonary TB in adults (Fine, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fine, 1995.

claim: CD8+ T cells can contribute to immune control of Mtb infection in mouse and non-human primate models of TB.
source: Multiple convergent lines of evidence from experiments in mouse and non-human primate models of TB show that CD8+ T cells can contribute to immune control of Mtb infection (Chen et al., 2009; Flynn et al., 1992; Woodworth et al., 2008b), but the antigenic targets of protective CD8+ T cell immunity to Mtb infection have not been conclusively defined.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009; Flynn et al., 1992; Woodworth et al., 2008b.

claim: CD8+ T cells specific for some immunodominant Mtb antigens poorly recognize Mtb-infected macrophages in murine models.
source: In murine models, CD8+ T cells specific for some immunodominant Mtb antigens poorly recognize Mtb-infected macrophages (Yang et al., 2018), implying that infected macrophages may not present all Mtb antigens that elicit cytokine-producing CD8+ T cell responses (Kamath et al., 2004; Lewinsohn et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: A high proportion of virulent Mtb remains intact and viable in macrophages.
source: Whereas some bacterial species are lysed following phagocytosis and expose their internal cell contents to antigen processing pathways (Shen et al., 1998), a high proportion of virulent Mtb remains intact and viable in macrophages (Armstrong and Hart, 1975; Lee et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2003), leading us to hypothesize that only a subset of Mtb proteins may be accessible for processing and presentation on MHC-I.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Armstrong and Hart, 1975; Lee et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2003.

claim: Primary human monocyte-derived macrophages were infected with Mtb H37Rv and MHC-I was isolated by immunoprecipitation 72 hours post-infection.
source: To identify Mtb antigens presented on MHC-I, we infected primary human monocyte-derived macrophages with Mtb H37Rv, isolated MHC-I by immunoprecipitation 72 hours post-infection, purified the associated peptides, and identified peptides by liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors.

claim: Thousands of peptides were identified for each primary cell donor, with a length distribution typical of MHC-I peptides.
source: We identified thousands of peptides for each primary cell donor, with a length distribution typical of MHC-I peptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and retention times that correlated well with hydrophobicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of identified peptides revealed groups corresponding to the known peptide sequence binding motifs of class I HLA alleles expressed by each donor.
source: Unsupervised clustering of identified peptides using GibbsCluster 2.0 (Andreatta et al., 2017) revealed groups corresponding to the known peptide sequence binding motifs of class I HLA alleles expressed by each donor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), confirming the specificity of our pulldowns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mtb peptides made up less than 0.1% of MHC-I peptides identified.
source: Mtb peptides made up less than 0.1% of MHC-I peptides identified, and this proportion was not discernibly increased by pre-treating macrophages with IFN-γ or treating with cycloheximide to inhibit host protein synthesis (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 77.85% of MASCOT identifications of putative Mtb peptides were rejected after manual data inspection.
source: 77.85% of MASCOT identifications of putative Mtb peptides were rejected after manual data inspection, and of the remaining candidates a further 51.51% were rejected following analysis by SureQuant (Table 2), highlighting the need for rigorous validation using best practices (Fritsche et al., 2021) when identifying pathogen-derived peptides among an MHC repertoire dominated by host-derived peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 2.

claim: Of the 16 Mtb-derived MHC-I peptides identified, 13 (81.25%) derived from proteins secreted via type VII secretion systems (T7SS).
source: Of the 16 Mtb-derived MHC-I peptides we identified, 13 (81.25%) derived from proteins secreted via type VII secretion systems (T7SS) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: T7SS substrates were significantly overrepresented in the MHC-I repertoire relative to the whole Mtb proteome at the peptide level (p<10–10).
source: T7SS substrates were significantly overrepresented in the MHC-I repertoire relative to the whole Mtb proteome, both at the peptide level (p<10–10; binomial test with Bonferroni correction) and at the protein level (p<10–7; hypergeometric test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: T7SS substrates were significantly overrepresented in the MHC-I repertoire relative to the whole Mtb proteome at the protein level (p<10–7).
source: T7SS substrates were significantly overrepresented in the MHC-I repertoire relative to the whole Mtb proteome, both at the peptide level (p<10–10; binomial test with Bonferroni correction) and at the protein level (p<10–7; hypergeometric test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Proteins without identifiable secretion signals were significantly underrepresented among Mtb-derived MHC-I peptides (p<10–8).
source: Proteins without identifiable secretion signals were significantly underrepresented among Mtb-derived MHC-I peptides (p<10–8; binomial test with Bonferroni correction) and source proteins (p<10–6; hypergeometric test with Bonferroni correction).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In a subset of macrophages at both early and late timepoints, a subset of Mtb co-localized with Galectin-3, a marker of phagosomal membrane permeabilization.
source: In a subset of macrophages at both early and late timepoints, a subset of Mtb co-localized with Galectin-3, a marker of phagosomal membrane permeabilization (Chauhan et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2012; Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, with citations to Chauhan et al., 2016 and Watson et al., 2012.

claim: A subset of Mtb co-localized with P62, an autophagy adaptor protein that recognizes cytosol-exposed bacteria.
source: A subset of Mtb also co-localized with P62, an autophagy adaptor protein that recognizes cytosol-exposed bacteria (Watson et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2009; Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, with citations to Watson et al., 2012 and Zheng et al., 2009.

claim: Mtb-containing phagosomes did not co-localize with MHC-I itself.
source: A subset of Mtb-containing phagosomes co-localized with the late endosome and lysosome marker LAMP-1 (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting access to endolysosomal proteases, but Mtb-containing phagosomes did not co-localize with MHC-I itself (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that Mtb antigens were unlikely to be loaded onto MHC-I in the Mtb-containing phagosome.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: An Mtb strain deficient in the activity of the ESX-1 secretion system (eccCa1:Tn) exhibited reduced co-localization with Galectin-3 and P62.
source: An Mtb strain deficient in the activity of the ESX-1 secretion system (eccCa1:Tn) exhibited reduced co-localization with Galectin-3 and P62 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: ESX-1 activity is required for Mtb to damage the phagosome membrane.
source: Our results are consistent with prior studies demonstrating that ESX-1 activity is required for Mtb to damage the phagosome membrane (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Simeone et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2012) and show that this phenomenon occurs in our primary human macrophage infection model.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2017; Simeone et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2012.

claim: Macrophages infected with ESX-1-deficient Mtb (eccCa1:Tn) did not present either EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I.
source: Targeted MS analysis revealed that macrophages infected with ESX-1-deficient Mtb (eccCa1:Tn) did not present either EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There was no difference in Mtb outgrowth between macrophages infected with wild-type or ESX-1-deficient Mtb.
source: We assessed alternative explanations for this difference in presentation of EsxA28-36 and EsxJKPW24-34 and observed no difference in Mtb outgrowth (Figure 3D), the proportion of cells infected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), or total MHC-I surface expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D) between macrophages infected with wild-type or ESX-1-deficient Mtb.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Addition of exogenous IFN-β restored a type I interferon response as measured by production of CXCL10.
source: Addition of exogenous IFN-β restored a type I interferon response as measured by production of CXCL10 (Figure 3E), but did not rescue presentation of EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Addition of exogenous IFN-β did not rescue presentation of EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I.
source: Addition of exogenous IFN-β restored a type I interferon response as measured by production of CXCL10 (Figure 3E), but did not rescue presentation of EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Presentation of EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I is dependent on ESX-1 activity but independent of downstream type I interferon signaling.
source: These results show that presentation of EsxA28-36 or EsxJKPW24-34 on MHC-I is dependent on ESX-1 activity but independent of downstream type I interferon signaling, consistent with a model in which ESX-1-mediated phagosomal damage enables Mtb antigens to access MHC-I antigen processing pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing ESX-1 dependence and IFN-β independence.

claim: Treatment with MG-132 inhibited proteasome activity, as measured by accumulation of proteins modified with K48-linked polyubiquitin.
source: Treatment with MG-132 inhibited proteasome activity, as measured by accumulation of proteins modified with K48-linked polyubiquitin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Treatment with E64d inhibited cathepsin B activity, as measured by a fluorometric assay.
source: Treatment with E64d inhibited cathepsin B activity, as measured by a fluorometric assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment with bafilomycin inhibited lysosomal acidification, as measured by lysotracker staining.
source: Treatment with bafilomycin inhibited lysosomal acidification, as measured by lysotracker staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Treatment with MG-132 and E64d each respectively reduced presentation of a subset of self MHC-I peptides but did not reduce presentation of Mtb peptides.
source: Treatment with MG-132 and E64d each respectively reduced presentation of a subset of self MHC-I peptides but did not reduce presentation of Mtb peptides (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment with bafilomycin broadly increased presentation of target MHC-I peptides.
source: Treatment with bafilomycin broadly increased presentation of target MHC-I peptides (Figure 4C). This increase was statistically significant for EsxA28-36 (Figure 4D; p<0.05, one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test), though not for EsxJKPW24-34 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increase in presentation with bafilomycin treatment was statistically significant for EsxA28-36 (p<0.05).
source: Treatment with bafilomycin broadly increased presentation of target MHC-I peptides (Figure 4C). This increase was statistically significant for EsxA28-36 (Figure 4D; p<0.05, one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparisons test), though not for EsxJKPW24-34 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BCG and Mtb H37Ra are both deficient in ESX-1 activity.
source: Given that we showed ESX-1 activity contributes to presentation of Mtb antigens in infection with virulent Mtb H37Rv, the fact that BCG and Mtb H37Ra are both deficient in ESX-1 activity (Frigui et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 1999; Guinn et al., 2004; Lewis et al., 2003; Pym et al., 2002) may in part explain this difference in the mycobacterial peptides presented on MHC-I.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frigui et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 1999; Guinn et al., 2004; Lewis et al., 2003; Pym et al., 2002.

claim: ESX-1 activity is not required for Mtb-infected human monocyte-derived dendritic cells to present an epitope derived from TB8.4 to cognate T cells.
source: ESX-1 activity is not required for Mtb-infected human monocyte-derived dendritic cells to present an epitope derived from TB8.4 (a Sec pathway substrate) to cognate T cells (Lewinsohn et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lewinsohn et al., 2006.

claim: ESX-1 activity is required for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for EsxB in vivo in mice.
source: While ESX-1 activity is required for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for EsxB in vivo in mice, it is dispensable for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for antigens exported via other secretion systems (such as TB8.4 and EsxH) (Woodworth et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Woodworth et al., 2008b.

claim: ESX-1 activity is dispensable for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for antigens exported via other secretion systems (such as TB8.4 and EsxH) in vivo in mice.
source: While ESX-1 activity is required for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for EsxB in vivo in mice, it is dispensable for priming of CD8+ T cell responses specific for antigens exported via other secretion systems (such as TB8.4 and EsxH) (Woodworth et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Woodworth et al., 2008b.

claim: In axenic culture, secretion of ESX-5 substrates is independent of ESX-1 function.
source: Whereas in axenic culture, secretion of ESX-5 substrates is independent of ESX-1 function (Champion et al., 2006; Shah and Briken, 2016), the fact that presentation of peptides derived from an ESX-5 substrate on MHC-I requires ESX-1 activity supports the hypothesis that the localization of secreted Mtb proteins within a host cell may depend on the activity of multiple T7SSs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Champion et al., 2006 and Shah and Briken, 2016.

claim: Presentation of peptides derived from an ESX-5 substrate on MHC-I requires ESX-1 activity.
source: Whereas in axenic culture, secretion of ESX-5 substrates is independent of ESX-1 function (Champion et al., 2006; Shah and Briken, 2016), the fact that presentation of peptides derived from an ESX-5 substrate on MHC-I requires ESX-1 activity supports the hypothesis that the localization of secreted Mtb proteins within a host cell may depend on the activity of multiple T7SSs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing ESX-1 dependence for ESX-5 substrate presentation.

claim: Mtb antigens must access the cytosol to be presented on MHC-I in human monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
source: Prior studies have shown that Mtb antigens must access the cytosol to be presented on MHC-I in human monocyte-derived dendritic cells (Grotzke et al., 2010; Grotzke et al., 2009; Lewinsohn et al., 2006), and our results are consistent with a model in which ESX-1-mediated phagosomal membrane damage enables Mtb antigens to access cytosolic antigen processing and presentation pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grotzke et al., 2010; Grotzke et al., 2009; Lewinsohn et al., 2006.

claim: In humans with prior exposure to Mtb, EsxA, EsxB, PPE51, and EsxJKPW are sources of immunodominant CD8+ T cell antigens.
source: Prior work shows that at least some of the MHC-I antigens we identified as potential vaccine targets are immunogenic in humans. Lewinsohn et al., 2017 showed that in humans with prior exposure to Mtb, EsxA, EsxB, PPE51, and EsxJKPW are sources of immunodominant CD8+ T cell antigens, while other antigens identified in our study elicited intermediate responses (PE13, PE35, PPE60, PPE19), and one elicited no detectable response (PPE20).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lewinsohn et al., 2017.

claim: CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells recognized multiple epitopes derived from EspC.
source: In a separate study, CD8+ T cells (as well as CD4+ T cells) recognized multiple epitopes derived from EspC (Millington et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Millington et al., 2011.

claim: EsxJ24-34 has been previously shown to be recognized by human T cells.
source: Individual peptides we identified by MS have also been previously shown to be recognized by human T cells, including EsxJ24-34 (Grotzke et al., 2010; Lewinsohn et al., 2013) and EsxA28-36 (Tully et al., 2005), providing a proof of concept that particular epitopes identified by MS can be immunogenic.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grotzke et al., 2010 and Lewinsohn et al., 2013.

claim: EsxA28-36 has been previously shown to be recognized by human T cells.
source: Individual peptides we identified by MS have also been previously shown to be recognized by human T cells, including EsxJ24-34 (Grotzke et al., 2010; Lewinsohn et al., 2013) and EsxA28-36 (Tully et al., 2005), providing a proof of concept that particular epitopes identified by MS can be immunogenic.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tully et al., 2005.

claim: Predicted class I HLA-binding motifs are statistically underrepresented in several Esx-family protein sequences.
source: Bioinformatic studies have also shown that predicted class I HLA-binding motifs are statistically underrepresented in several Esx-family protein sequences, suggesting that these proteins may be under selective pressure to escape recognition by CD8+ T cells (Maman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maman et al., 2011.
